489.history: The river port at the mouth of the Abhainn naomh was the town the Sundering was made in. In its harbour-house, Taigh a' Chalaidh, Calum mac Nèill opened the roll of the willing in the second year and wrote every household whole or not at all, cutting a struck name through with one stroke rather than scraping it. Alasdair Saor laid the first deep keel on the strand below the town, the fellowship of the strand swore its apprentices over a coal, and the queen's masons lengthened the west quay in dressed stone for what the crown called the harbour's trade. On the night before the sailing a lamp stood in every window along the waterfront, and in the morning Calum's grandson Niall cut one notch on a hazel stick for every hull that went round the river pool sunwise and down to the sea. The quay was called Cidhe an Diosail after that, and its old name passed to a fish-wharf. The harbour carried half its old trade within a generation. Mànas mac Ruairidh preached Manannan on its stones in the seventh century of the count, and Taigh Mhanannain was raised beside the harbour-court. Its synod set the prayer for the shut sea at the foot of the river pool. The night of lamps thinned household by household until one old woman, Ealasaid nic Iain, kept the last lamp; eleven people stood on the quay at the last rite of the empty harbour the age records, and the harbour scribe Eòghann mac Nèill counted them.
489.known_for: the roll of the willing, Cidhe an Diosail and the night of lamps

19.history: The kings and queens of the age kept their hall on the Red Hill above the Abhainn dhomhain, and every crowning of the age was made there. Beathag nic Dhòmhnaill heard the three crews in the red hall in the first year, gave her word that the crown would send no one and keep no one back, and wore undyed wool for her sister from the thirteenth year of the count until she died in the fifty-fifth. The houses first chose a king here when Ìomhar's line failed, in a cold yard where seven neck-rings caught the sun and nobody spoke for a morning. Sìleas set the standard firlot here and widened the bridge for two carts abreast; Catrìona Bhuadhach laid her stone road south from it to Inis thais. The crown was joined to the mastery of the vein-house in Dòmhnall Ruadh's reign, and from then the red hall's letters carried the custody's seal. The capital grew slowly and Cathair mhòr passed it in the tenth century of the count; in the age's last years the hall held perhaps five hundred souls. After Queen Gormshuil went up to the winter burning in LE 1,795 and nothing more is told, the seven houses sat at her board with her chair left empty, and named themselves Comhairle a' Chùraim there in LE 1,812.
19.known_for: the red hall, the queen's empty chair, and the board of the seven houses

55.history: The fishing village a little below Seann Skell gave more households to the roll of the willing than any other place on the island. Two of its households said in the drying-shed, in the first year, that they would go if a boat were ever built that could make the crossing, and the village laughed and then stopped laughing. Mòrag nic Dhòmhnaill and her husband Aonghas mac Fhionnlaigh farmed the land above it, and it was at their board that Alasdair Saor was sent north to the oaks of Doire fhionn. When the trial hull An Fhaoileag lay down off Ros àrsaidh in the sixth year, its boats brought back three living and eight dead; the roll-keeper cut eleven names on the village's board in one night, and a lamp burned on the shingle for the three the sea kept. When the broken tidings of two landfalls came, the village kept both halves of the tale at once. Ruairidh mac Artair had a deep hull built here in the fourth century of the count; it listed at launch and was broken up within a fortnight, for no wright still living held the old scarfing of the keel.
55.known_for: the eleven names on its board, and the households it gave to the fleet

122.history: The small walled harbour on the point below Ros bheag is where the ships of Inis àrsaidh put out to sea. The first finished hull, An Fhaoileag, was taken past it for her trial in the sixth year and lay down in a following sea off its headland with fourteen aboard. Eight years later its strand was the ground of the first night-steering trial, when Catrìona nic Iain, home from the steersmen of Cuan ruadh, took one boat out past the headland with every lantern doused and brought her in by Reul na Stiùire before the lantern-boat that hugged the shore. Half the town came down to see it fail. After the fleet sailed the point went back to the coasting trade and the fishing, and nobody out of it is recorded to have sailed by night again.
122.known_for: the loss of An Fhaoileag, and the first night steered by a star

282.history: The harbour a dozen miles down the coast from Seann Skell heard the first tale of a far shore on its quays in the moon of Faolach of the first year, and its skipper Eachann mac Lachlainn told the queen of a low dark coast west and north of west. For the fleet it gave its hemp fields to cordage, and by the sixth year its waterfront was three rope-walks end to end, where Iain Ròpaire and his walkers learned the names of a keel so that the shroud-lines would stop failing. The walks turned off hands when the harbour trade halved after the sailing, and were shortened in the eighth century of the count, half the ground sown with barley. The rope-walker Tormod Ciar swore the Cup of Manannan on the walk itself, cupping rainwater in his hands. In the fourteenth century Tormod Ròpaire's crew still walked their strands to a work-song whose strange words named the parts of a deep keel, and Iseabail nic Lachlainn took it down there; the crew kept singing it exactly as he gave it, no better understood.

63.history: The walled harbour town of the Ros bheag cape sent its skipper Oighrig nic Raghnaill to the red hall in the first year with a telling of a high forested coast past the north cape, and two of the six pilots who walked east to learn the stars at Cuan ruadh were its own, Catrìona nic Iain among them. After the sailing it was a fishing and coasting town like its neighbours. Manannan's teaching came to it down the coast with the fishing families, and in LE 694 the priests of the order at Ros bheag laid down that no boat of the faithful might go out of sight of the headlands; within the year two of the order's boats turned back its own skipper Coinneach mac Sheumais when he chased a run of fish too far. Four years later a priest there asked a pilot's grandson, Griogair, which star his grandfather had steered by, and the boy could not say. The rule of the headlands was kept on the west coast for the rest of the age.
63.known_for: the rule of sight-of-land, and the pilot who forgot his star

420.history: The shire seat a little north of Cuan shean raised the sail-cloth for the fleet. Its tally-keeper cut a notch on his sticks for every close-woven length delivered from the households of Siorrachd Baile àrsaidh, owed once and reckoned against nothing, and by the ninth year he had cut more notches than he had thought the shire held households, some from weavers with no kin on the roll and no thought of sailing. The sticks filled a chest that wanted a second lid. After the sailing the shire went back to weaving for its own backs and the coasting trade, and the levy-chest is remembered in the shire as the one thing it ever gave that it did not count the cost of.
420.known_for: the sail-cloth levy for the fleet

64.history: The walled port nearest the capital on the west keeps salt-pans and brine springs behind its walls, and they fed it through the War of the Three Claimants. Its reeve Mairead nic Ruairidh gave the heralds of all three claimants the same answer at the western gate: the town would open to trade and shut to hosts until the houses agreed which claim to answer. Dùghall Garbh sat before it a fortnight in LE 553, and Mairead sold his host bread at the market rate until his carters cost him more than the town was worth; he came back better provisioned three years later and sat a month, and marched away when Catrìona closed the gates of Cathair dhomhain. In LE 594 Catrìona Bhuadhach granted Seann Warr the right to keep its own gates and take its own tolls, and the grant was cut in stone letters over the landward gate.
64.known_for: the gate shut against all three claimants, and the grant cut over it

35.history: A wood of wild oak, crooked and never anyone's grove, stood on the shore of Loch chrom below the capital, and in the fifth year woodcutters of the roll built huts at its edge to fell crooked oak for the fleet's frames and knees. The huts did not outlast the felling. The wood kept its name, and the tellers of that shore say that timber for the fleet was felled there. Fifteen centuries on, other woodcutters came to what was left of the wood and stayed, and their huts became the village of Doire fhiadhaich, a fishing and cutting place on the capital shore that remembered the fleet chiefly as a reason for its name.
35.known_for: its oaks, said to have built the Sundering fleet

26.history: The walled harbour city above the river mouth, with its citadel of the Holy Age and granaries deep enough for two winters, declared for Dùghall Garbh in the second year of the War of the Three Claimants, chiefly because its harbour-master had once carried grain for him. Catrìona nic Aonghais came against it in the autumn of LE 556; borrowed fishing coasters shut its water gate by night while her lines held the land gate. With no ground beyond the walls for burying, the dead were laid near the well-heads, and a sickness of the gut went through the streets and the garrison. On the fortieth day Niall Mòr mac Leòid surrendered, and Catrìona let his garrison march out between her silent lines on his sworn word, carrying its dead and wounded by name. It was in her camp before this city that Dùghall Garbh came with six men and no herald to offer her his host against Raghnall Ruadh.
26.known_for: the siege of forty days and the garrison freed on oath
